extracted.intended_audience: British public, legislators, and readers of political pamphlets debating the principles of the French Revolution and the English Constitution
extracted.subtask_description: A polemical constitutional argument defending hereditary succession, the settled statutes of 1688 and subsequent settlement, and arguing against doctrines of popular election, cashiering rulers, and revolutionary pulpit agitation. The text lays out legal, historical, and prudential reasons to prefer hereditary continuity and parliamentary safeguards over popular elective theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three claimed rights of the Revolution Society
rubrics_metrics.description: The Revolution (Society) asserts that the people of England have acquired a right (1) to choose their own governors, (2) to cashier them for misconduct, and (3) to frame a government for themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author presents these three as the central doctrinal claims of the Society, but contends they belong to a faction only, that the body of the people disclaims them, and that their practical assertion will be resisted. The entry functions as a statement of the contested proposition that the remainder of the text seeks to refute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaration of Right (1688) contains no right to elect governors
rubrics_metrics.description: The Declaration of Right (the act of the 1st of William and Mary) contains no word or suggestion of a general right 'to choose our own governors,' 'to cashier them for misconduct,' or 'to form a government for ourselves.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues that the Declaration ties 'rights and succession' together and was deliberately drafted by experienced lawyers and statesmen to preserve hereditary succession rather than establish an elective principle. Use this document-based reading to refute claims that 1688 created a general elective right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certainty of succession is essential for unity, peace, and tranquillity
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'certainty in the succession' of the crown is necessary for the unity, peace, and tranquillity of the nation; the statute language links the protection of liberties with an established hereditary succession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted legislative phrases emphasize that preserving certainty of succession was seen as material to national security. The author uses this legal and prudential claim to argue electoral doctrines would undermine national stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special-case deviations (exceptional acts) do not create general legal principles
rubrics_metrics.description: A law or decision made in a special case (e.g., the temporary acceptance of William) should not be generalized into a universal principle: 'Privilegium non transit in exemplum.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author warns against deriving a standing rule (elective monarchy) from an exceptional, necessity-driven act. Historical examples (William's accession, Lord Somers' wording) are used to show the legislature treated the event as an exception, not a new rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral competence of constituent bodies is limited; parts cannot abdicate permanent authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Constituent parts of the state (e.g., the House of Lords, House of Commons) are not morally competent to dissolve themselves, abdicate their legislative functions, or surrender public faith—such surrender would violate the constitutional pact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle restricts how much a branch may change its own role; it is used to argue against radical reorganization by transient majorities. The author contrasts abstract sovereign competence with moral/constitutional limits that bind institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use parliamentary and legal mechanisms rather than vague 'cashiering' for misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Removing rulers for 'misconduct' is too loose and indefinite to be a constitutional principle; instead the Revolution-era statutes provided safeguards such as ministerial responsibility, frequent meetings of Parliament, impeachment, and limits on royal pardons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that 'cashiering governors' is imprecise and dangerous; historical statutes and mechanisms (e.g., no pardon under great seal pleadable to an impeachment) are preferable and more legally sound ways to secure liberties.

rubrics_metrics.name: The king is a sovereign lord under the law, not a removable 'servant of the people'
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Constitution the king is legally 'our sovereign lord the king' who is not ordinarily obedient to any other person; to call him a servant removable at will misconceives his constitutional role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a rebuttal of rhetorical formulations (e.g., 'servant of the people') that would imply easy removability; the author treats such language as both ineffective flattery and a threat to constitutional order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of elective-only legitimacy would invalidate prior lawful acts and statutes
rubrics_metrics.description: If no throne is lawful except by elective title, then prior monarchs who were not popularly chosen would be treated as usurpers and the statutes enacted under them (e.g., Petition of Right, Habeas Corpus) would be thrown into doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author uses this reductio to show practical absurdities and legal chaos that would follow from adopting an absolutist elective principle; the criterion is thus a test of doctrinal consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act of Settlement (12 & 13 William) binds heirs and posterity to hereditary Protestant succession
rubrics_metrics.description: The act (12th and 13th of King William) was intended to bind 'us, and our heirs, and our posterity' to the Protestant line, securing an hereditary crown and hereditary allegiance by statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author points to the statute's explicit terms (naming Sophia as stock/root) as evidence Parliament deliberately entrenched hereditary succession despite foreignness or inconvenience, demonstrating policy preference for continuity over election.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conserve-and-correct principle: limit changes to the defective parts, preserve existing constitutional fabric
rubrics_metrics.description: In times of emergency a state should repair or replace only the defective part of the constitution while preserving the rest of the edifice, rather than dissolving the whole and creating a new civil order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical practice at the Restoration and the Revolution is cited as models: change by regeneration of deficient parts through unimpaired old parts. This serves as a procedural/prudential rule for constitutional reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cashiering or deposing a king ordinarily requires force and becomes a case of war, not constitutional remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: The ceremony of cashiering kings can rarely be performed without force; when force is used laws and tribunals are silenced and the event becomes war rather than a constitutional process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a warning about the practical means and likely violent consequences of attempting to depose a sovereign outside established legal procedures; the text treats this as an anti-pattern for resolving alleged misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid revolutionary pulpit rhetoric and importing foreign fashions of liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: Preachers and 'new evangelists' should not turn pulpits into platforms for radical political doctrines or import foreign (French) revolutionary fashions which are alien to British constitutional practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author criticizes the habit of using pulpit eloquence to acclimatize congregations to dangerous political theories, describing the importation and re-exportation of 'counterfeit wares' of liberty as an illicit and mischievous practice.
